facts.claim: "Bow Down" (feat. Amaarae) is track 9 on SPINALL's album TOP BOY, released 17 February 2023, and runs 2:03.
The song was released by TheCAPMusic as part of the album Top Boy.
The songwriters are Ama Serwah Genfi (Amaarae) and Sodamola Oluseye Desmond (Spinall).
Spinall is the sole credited producer of "Bow Down".
Afrocritik called the track slightly disappointing, saying its sparse instrumentals did not quite match Amaarae's sonic presence.
iMullar praised Amaarae's performance, citing trumpet horns in the production and a second verse that marks her as one of the voices of alternative music. It named the song a standout on the album.
African Folder reads the song as Spinall's nod to the alté movement, since it enlists the Ghanaian singer Amaarae.
Spinall told Apple Music that the album title Top Boy was inspired by people who have beaten the odds and used the resources available to them to succeed.
Top Boy is Spinall's sixth studio album. Its lead single was a remix of "Sere", a track from his previous album Grace.
Spinall is a Nigerian DJ and producer who brands his style TheCAP (The CrazyAzzParty). His career includes an Atlantic Records UK deal and his 2015 debut album My Story.

research.lineage: The song sits in contemporary Nigerian and pan-African DJ-curated afrobeats, with an alté (alternative Afro-fusion) guest turn from Ghanaian singer Amaarae.

draft:
The whole song turns on a request that sounds like a command until you hear the last word. "Make me bow down / To it please," Amaarae sings at the end of each refrain. That "please" gives it away. The narrator has spent the verses sounding like the most powerful person in the room. Here she asks to be overpowered, and she's polite about it.

**Bow Down** is track nine on SPINALL's sixth album, *TOP BOY*. Spinall produced it alone and wrote it with Amaarae. He has said the album's title honors people who beat the odds with whatever they had on hand. The song's opening fits that brief in its own way. It asks for money in naira, cedis and dollars, Nigerian and Ghanaian currency next to the American kind, and it wants more, not less. Pleasure and enjoyment are named as the reason for being here. It's a pan-African wish list, delivered with the ease of someone who expects to get it.

Then the song slides from wealth into worship. Amaarae calls herself the holy spirit to the godless and warns off anyone trying "witchy witchy" tricks. In the hook a lover asks her to whine her waist, and the moment flips the religious language around: "Feels like Gods giving praise to me." She isn't the one praying. She's the one being prayed to. A few lines later she admits she's lost in the sauce and lost in her thoughts, a slave to the very thing she controls. Pride and surrender sit in the same four bars, and the song never chooses between them.

The second verse is pure play: a Bee Gees joke, Fiji Water as a swimming pool, a wink that none of this stays PG. iMullar singled out that verse as the moment Amaarae proves she's one of alternative music's key voices, and named the track a standout. African Folder heard Spinall nodding to the alté scene by bringing in the Ghanaian singer. Afrocritik was cooler, finding the production too sparse to match her presence. iMullar heard trumpet horns in it.

That disagreement is part of the appeal. This is a DJ's record that leaves room for a guest to take it over, and Amaarae does. At two minutes it's a quick visit, two verses and a chant, with no time to explain itself.

What sticks is that "please": a voice sure enough of its own divinity to beg for someone who can bring it to its knees, and you end up wanting that too.

factCheck.note: Matches the lyrics exactly and the lines recur at the end of each Bow Down chant.
